An apostrophe shows ownership. It goes on the owner, never on the thing that's owned.
Here's the method. First ask: is the next word owned? If not, there's no apostrophe at all. If it is, count the owners.
One owner gets apostrophe s. The author's political writings. One author owns the writings.
Trap alert. Authors apostrophe, writings apostrophe? There's only one author, and the writings don't own anything. Never put the apostrophe on the thing owned.
More than one owner ending in s gets s apostrophe. Rice and tomatoes: the two plants' genetic profiles.
A plural that doesn't end in s, like children, just adds apostrophe s. The children's books. Childrens apostrophe is not a word.
And if nothing is owned, there's no apostrophe. The scientists collected samples. Plain plural.
Pronouns are different. Its, their, and whose own things with no apostrophe. It's with an apostrophe only ever means it is. They're only means they are.
Test it out loud. Read it as: a butterfly flapping, it is, wings. That's nonsense. So use its, with no apostrophe.
Let's try an SAT style question. Two paintings are similar in blank use of large canvases. Their, they're, there, or their apostrophe?
Read they're as they are: similar in they are use. Nonsense. The paintings own the use, so the answer is their.
Trap alert. Their apostrophe is never correct. Pronouns never take an apostrophe to show owning.
Your turn. Pause the video. The three students blank projects were displayed. Student's, or students'?
Students'. Three students, more than one owner ending in s, so s apostrophe.
Remember three things. Ask if the next word is owned. Count the owners: one gets apostrophe s, many get s apostrophe. And pronouns never use an apostrophe to own. Great work.
